methods.label: Extract a square from each product
methods.explanation:
Recall that \(n!=1\cdot2\cdots n\). Instead of calculating these enormous factorials, expand the larger factorial just far enough to obtain two copies of the smaller one. Using \(99!=99\cdot98!\), \(100!=100\cdot99!\), and \(101!=101\cdot100!\), the choices become
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{A}:&\quad 11(3\cdot98!)^2,\\
\text{B}:&\quad 11(30\cdot98!)^2,\\
\text{C}:&\quad (10\cdot99!)^2,\\
\text{D}:&\quad 101(10\cdot99!)^2,\\
\text{E}:&\quad 101(100!)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
In a perfect square, each prime occurs an even number of times, because squaring doubles every prime exponent. Multiplying a square by the prime \(11\) or \(101\) makes that prime's exponent odd. Therefore A, B, D, and E are not squares.

Choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\) is a perfect square, since \(99!\cdot100!=(10\cdot99!)^2\).
